title: Cap. X Ultimum: Major consequence — absolute predestination is mercy’s preparation of grace that leads to glory; Vossius wrongly makes efficacious grace Augustine’s peculiarity
latin: De consequentia Majoris non necesse est ut multis agatur. Nam qui concedit efficacem gratiam ex Dei beneplacito praeparari et donari quibusdam nihilo aliis dignioribus, nec ulla praevia operatione bona distantibus ab illis quibus eadem negatur, is doctrinam absolutae electionis et praeteritionis, si consequenter loqui velit, non potest negare. Quid enim aliud intelligimus per praedestinationem absolutam quam gratiae ad gloriam efficaciter perducentis ex mera misericordia praeparationem? et per reprobationem huic absolutae praedestinationi oppositam, quam talis gratiae ex liberrima Dei voluntate negatam praeparationem? In hoc itaque etsi minime vera, tamen sibi consentanea est doctissimi viri Gerardi Vossii, qui Historiam Pelagianam conscripsit, sententia, quando sicuti doctrinam de absoluta praedestinatione, ita et hanc de efficaci gratia quibusdam ex absoluto Dei decreto praeparata, quibusdam non praeparata, Augustini peculiarem facit, et aliorum Orthodoxorum qui Pelagio restiterunt minime communem.
pass_a: Concerning the consequence of the Major it is not needful that it be treated with many words. For he who grants that efficacious grace is prepared and given from God’s good pleasure unto certain ones no whit worthier than others, nor differing by any previous good operation from those unto whom the same is denied, cannot, if he will speak consistently, deny the doctrine of absolute election and preterition. For what else do we understand by absolute predestination than the preparation from mere mercy of grace effectively leading unto glory? and by reprobation opposite unto this absolute predestination, than the denied preparation of such grace from God’s freest will? In this therefore, though by no means true, yet consistent with itself is the sentence of that most learned man Gerard Vossius, who wrote the Pelagian History, when as he makes the doctrine of absolute predestination, so also this of efficacious grace prepared for certain ones from God’s absolute decree, not prepared for certain, peculiar unto Augustine, and by no means common unto the other Orthodox who withstood Pelagius.
pass_b: The Major’s consequence needs few words. Whoever grants that efficacious grace is prepared and given from God’s good pleasure to some no worthier than others, and not set apart by any prior good act from those denied the same, cannot—if he would speak consistently—deny absolute election and preterition. What else is absolute predestination but mercy’s preparation of the grace that leads effectively to glory? And what else is reprobation opposite to that but the free denial of preparing such grace? So Gerard Vossius’s view in his Pelagian History, though untrue, is at least consistent with itself when he makes not only absolute predestination but also efficacious grace prepared for some by absolute decree and not for others peculiar to Augustine, not common to the other Orthodox who withstood Pelagius.

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1 open: Orthodox Grace of Christ is healing, regenerating, creating the good will—not merely illuminating, exciting, knocking
latin: Missa igitur Majoris consequentia, de tribus illis propositionibus, quas diximus communi Orthodoxorum consensu contra Pelagianos fuisse stabilitas, disseremus. Prima haec est: Orthodoxi per Gratiam Christi, quam Pelagius nunquam fateri voluit, intellexerunt non illuminantem, excitantem, pulsantem gratiam, et sese intromitti ab humana voluntate quasi petentem, sed sanantem, vivificantem, regenerantem, aditum sibi facientem, uno verbo, fidem et charitatem inspirantem, ac ipsam bonam voluntatem de novo creantem. Tria hic expendemus: 1. Qualem gratiam ipse Pelagius tandem agnoverit. 2. Qualem noluerit unquam admittere. 3. Qualis ea fuerit quam Patres gratiam Christi κατ' ἐξοχήν vocarunt, atque ad cujus confessionem Pelagium adigere voluerunt.
pass_a: The consequence of the Major therefore being dismissed, we will treat of those three propositions which we said were established by the common consent of the Orthodox against the Pelagians. The first is this: The Orthodox understood by the Grace of Christ, which Pelagius never willed to confess, not an illuminating, exciting, knocking grace, and as it were begging to be let in by the human will, but a healing, quickening, regenerating grace, making an entrance for itself—in a word, inspiring faith and charity, and creating the good will itself anew. Here we will weigh three things: 1. What grace Pelagius himself at length acknowledged. 2. What he never willed to admit. 3. What that was which the Fathers called the Grace of Christ by excellence, and unto whose confession they willed to drive Pelagius.
pass_b: Setting the Major’s consequence aside, we will treat the three propositions we said the Orthodox settled by common consent against the Pelagians. First: by the Grace of Christ—which Pelagius never would confess—the Orthodox meant not a grace that only lights, stirs, and knocks, waiting to be let in by the human will, but a healing, quickening, regenerating grace that forces its own entrance—in a word, breathing in faith and charity and creating the good will itself anew. We will weigh three points: (1) what grace Pelagius finally acknowledged; (2) what he never would admit; (3) what the Fathers called the Grace of Christ by excellence, and to whose confession they meant to drive him.

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1.I: Pelagius grants supernatural grace only as law and external teaching — Aug. De grat. Christi 3; Prosper De Ingratis
latin: I. Concessit igitur Pelagius supernaturalem gratiam, sed in doctrina constitutam, sive revelatione externa earum rerum quae ad salutem consequendam sunt necessaria. Patet ex Augustino, lib. 1. De gratia Christi contra Pelag. cap. 3. Gratiam Dei aut in natura ponit, aut in lege atque doctrina: ut cum adjuvet Deus hominem, revelando et ostendendo quid fieri debeat, adjuvare credatur. Idem videre licet apud Prosperum, Carmine De Ingratis, cap. 20. Aliud non est vobiscum gratia quam lex, quamque propheta monens, et quam doctrina ministri. Et in Epistola ad Ruff. De grat. et lib. arbitr. Hoc tantum dicit eos de gratia confiteri, quod quaedam libero arbitrio sit magistra, etc. Sed Orthodoxi hac gratia externa et monitrice minime contenti, urgebant internam gratiam esse agnoscendam.
pass_a: I. Pelagius therefore granted supernatural grace, but constituted in doctrine, or in the external revelation of those things which are necessary unto obtaining salvation. It is plain from Augustine, lib. 1. De gratia Christi contra Pelag. cap. 3. He places the grace of God either in nature, or in law and doctrine: so that when God helps a man, by revealing and showing what ought to be done, he is believed to help. The same may be seen in Prosper, in the Poem De Ingratis, cap. 20. Grace with you is nothing other than law, and the warning prophet, and the teaching of a minister. And in the Epistle to Ruffinus De grat. et lib. arbitr. He says they confess only this concerning grace, that it is a certain mistress unto free will, etc. But the Orthodox, by no means content with this external and admonishing grace, urged that internal grace must be acknowledged.
pass_b: I. Pelagius granted supernatural grace—but as doctrine, or external revelation of what is needed for salvation. Augustine makes it plain (De gratia Christi contra Pelagium 1.3): he puts God’s grace either in nature or in law and teaching, so that God is thought to help by revealing and showing what ought to be done. Prosper says the same (De Ingratis 20): With you grace is nothing but law, the warning prophet, and a minister’s teaching. And in the letter to Ruffinus on grace and free will he says they confess only that grace is somehow a mistress to free will. The Orthodox, not content with that external admonishing grace, pressed that internal grace must be acknowledged.

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1.I cont.: Pelagius then grants internal illuminating and exciting grace by persuasion — still not healing the will
latin: Agnovit igitur Pelagius et gratiam internam: Primo, illuminantem et aperientem oculos mentis. Clara sunt illa verba ejus apud Augustinum, De grat. Christi cap. 7. Adjuvat nos Deus per doctrinam et revelationem suam, dum cordis nostri oculos aperit, dum nos multiformi et ineffabili dono gratiae caelestis illuminat. Secundo, concedit gratiam internam excitantem affectus, et excutere conantem voluntati torporem suum, mediante illuminatione praedicta, et antecedente suasione quadam arcana. Huc spectant illa, Ibid. cap. 10. Operatur in nobis velle quod bonum est, dum nos terrenis cupiditatibus deditos futurae gloriae magnitudine et praemiorum pollicitatione accendit; dum revelatione sapientiae in desiderium Dei stupentem suscitat voluntatem; dum nobis suadet omne quod bonum est. Huc usque perductus est ipse Pelagius.
pass_a: Pelagius therefore acknowledged internal grace also: First, illuminating and opening the eyes of the mind. Clear are those words of his in Augustine, De grat. Christi cap. 7. God helps us by his doctrine and revelation, while he opens the eyes of our heart, while he illuminates us with the manifold and ineffable gift of heavenly grace. Secondly, he grants an internal grace exciting the affections, and striving to shake off the will’s torpor, by means of the foresaid illumination, and by a certain secret preceding persuasion. Unto this look those words, Ibid. cap. 10. He works in us to will what is good, while he kindles us, given over to earthly desires, by the greatness of future glory and the promise of rewards; while by revelation of wisdom he raises the astonished will unto desire of God; while he persuades us of everything that is good. Unto this point Pelagius himself was brought.
pass_b: So Pelagius also granted internal grace—first illuminating, opening the mind’s eyes. His words in Augustine (De gratia Christi 7) are clear: God helps us by his teaching and revelation when he opens our heart’s eyes and lights us with heaven’s manifold, unspeakable gift. Second, he grants an internal grace that stirs the affections and tries to shake torpor from the will, by that illumination and by a prior secret persuasion. So ibid. 10: He works in us to will the good when he kindles us, given to earthly desires, with future glory’s greatness and the promise of rewards; when by wisdom’s revelation he raises the stunned will to desire God; when he persuades us of all that is good. That far Pelagius himself was led.

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1.II: Pelagius refuses the grace that heals and turns the will by infusing faith and charity — leaves the will in indifference
latin: II. Jam, secundo in loco videamus qualem noluit admittere. Breviter dico: Illam gratiam Dei noluit Pelagius, quae sua efficacitate sanaret voluntatem, et ex mala in bonam commutaret, infundendo illi fidem, charitatem, reliquaque quae vitam spiritualem et salutem aeternam secum apportant: sed admisit eam solummodo (ut dictum est) quae illuminat mentem, movet affectus, invitat voluntatem; ita tamen ut eam permittat sibi, et ab aequilibrio indifferentiae suae non dimoveat, exspectans scilicet ab ipsa voluntate actum credendi, convertendi, ac consimilia, non operans in ipsa hosce actus.
pass_a: II. Now, in the second place let us see what he willed not to admit. Briefly I say: Pelagius willed not that grace of God which by its efficacy would heal the will, and change it from evil unto good, by infusing into it faith, charity, and the rest which bring with them spiritual life and everlasting salvation: but he admitted only that (as has been said) which illuminates the mind, moves the affections, invites the will; yet so that it leaves the will to itself, and does not move it from the balance of its indifference, waiting namely from the will itself for the act of believing, of converting, and the like, not working these acts in it.
pass_b: II. Second: what he would not admit. Briefly: Pelagius refused the grace that by its efficacy heals the will and turns it from evil to good by pouring in faith, charity, and the rest that bring spiritual life and everlasting salvation. He admitted only what lights the mind, moves the affections, and invites the will—yet so as to leave the will to itself and not shift it from indifference’s balance, waiting on the will for the act of believing, converting, and the like, not working those acts in it.

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1.II: Augustine, Jerome’s Critobolus, Julian — help only to be able; Semipelagians likewise withhold the gift of willing itself
latin: Sic ejus sententiam expressit Augustinus, De grat. Christi, cap. 5. Scire debemus, quod nec voluntatem nostram nec actionem Divino adjuvari credit auxilio, sed solum possibilitatem voluntatis atque operis. Et paulo post, Non adjuvat ut velimus, non adjuvat ut agamus, sed tantummodo adjuvat ut velle et agere valeamus. Sic Critobolus ille qui apud Hieronymum sustinet personam Pelagiani, Dialog. advers. Pelag. lib. 3. Non tollo, inquit, Dei auxilium, quippe per cujus gratiam possumus omne quod possumus, sed utrumque suis finibus terminamus, ut et Dei sit gratia quod dedit libero arbitrio potestatem, et nostrae voluntatis facere quid vel non facere. Et hoc est quod Julianus dixit, Voluntatem humanam operis boni existentiam a se accipere. In hunc eundem scopulum impegerunt et Semipelagiani: Nam gratiam Dei praevenientem concedentes, talem tamen fingunt quae non det ipsum Velle, ipsum Credere, ipsum Perseverare; sed quae eventum semper committat libero arbitrio per gratiam Dei excitato et adjuto.
pass_a: Thus Augustine expressed his sentence, De grat. Christi, cap. 5. We ought to know that he believes neither our will nor our action to be helped by Divine aid, but only the possibility of will and of work. And a little after, He does not help that we may will, he does not help that we may act, but only helps that we may be able to will and to act. So that Critobolus who in Jerome sustains the Pelagian’s person, Dialog. advers. Pelag. lib. 3. I do not take away, he says, God’s help, seeing that by his grace we can all that we can, but we bound each within its limits, so that it is God’s grace that he gave power unto free will, and of our will to do or not to do. And this is what Julian said, that the human will receives from itself the existence of a good work. Upon this same rock the Semipelagians also struck: For granting God’s preventing grace, they yet invent such as does not give Willing itself, Believing itself, Persevering itself; but which always commits the event unto free will stirred and helped by God’s grace.
pass_b: So Augustine puts his view (De gratia Christi 5): We should know he thinks divine aid helps neither our will nor our act, but only the possibility of willing and working. A little later: He does not help so that we will, nor so that we act—only so that we are able to will and act. Jerome’s Critobolus, speaking as a Pelagian (Dialogi adversus Pelagianos 3), says: I do not remove God’s help, for by his grace we can all we can; but we keep each in its bounds—God’s grace that he gave free will power, and our will to do or not do. That is Julian’s point: the human will takes from itself the existence of a good work. The Semipelagians hit the same rock: granting preventing grace, they still invent a grace that does not give Willing, Believing, Persevering themselves, but always leaves the event to free will stirred and helped by God’s grace.

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1: Hilary and Faustus; then Arminius/Arnoldus reject the grace that makes the good will — only sweet persuasion, event to free will
latin: Sic Hilarius in Epist. ad August. Illud testimonium, Sicut unicuique partitus est mensuram fidei, et similia, ad id volunt valere, ut adjuvetur qui coeperit velle, non ut etiam donetur ut velit. Paulo post, Rationem reddunt electorum vel rejectorum ex eo, quod unicuique meritum propriae voluntatis adjungitur. Denique Faustus Rhegiensis Semipelagianorum coryphaeus, Divinae, inquit, miserationis est ut voceris, sed tuae voluntati commissum ut sequaris, Pag. 1493. Voluntatem ejus qui est purgandus exspectat Deus, Pag. 1506. Hujusmodi innumera apud hunc auctorem occurrunt, ex quibus colligimus Pelagianos et Semipelagianos in hoc conspirasse, quod numquam concedere voluerunt specialem Dei munificentiam et misericordiam, qua infundatur fides et charitas aliquibus, bonaque voluntas eo pacto in iisdem creetur. Jam superpondii loco et illud apponemus: Arminium ac Arnoldum, caeterosque qui ex eadem Schola prodierunt, non agnoscere illam quam Pelagiani et Semipelagiani exploserunt, nempe illam quae sua efficacitate bonam voluntatem facit; sed illam solam quae suasione movet ut bona esse velit, eventum autem ipsi libero arbitrio commitit.
pass_a: So Hilary in the Epistle to Augustine. That testimony, As he has dealt to every man the measure of faith, and the like, they will to have avail unto this, that he who has begun to will is helped, not that it is also given that he may will. A little after, They render the reason of elect or rejected from this, that unto each the merit of his own will is joined. Finally Faustus of Riez, the Semipelagians’ coryphaeus, It is of Divine pity, he says, that thou art called, but committed unto thy will that thou follow, Pag. 1493. God waits for the will of him who is to be purged, Pag. 1506. Innumerable of this kind occur in this author, from which we gather that Pelagians and Semipelagians conspired in this, that they never willed to grant God’s special munificence and mercy by which faith and charity are infused into some, and a good will is thereby created in the same. Now in the place of a makeweight we will also set this: that Arminius and Arnoldus, and the rest who have come forth from the same School, do not acknowledge that which the Pelagians and Semipelagians exploded, namely that which by its efficacy makes the good will; but only that which by persuasion moves that it may will to be good, but commits the event unto free will itself.
pass_b: So Hilary to Augustine: texts like As he has dealt to each the measure of faith they take to mean the one who has begun to will is helped—not that willing itself is given. A little later: they explain elect and rejected by the merit of each one’s own will joined on. Faustus of Riez, the Semipelagians’ chief, says (p. 1493): It is of divine pity that you are called, but left to your will that you follow; and (p. 1506): God waits for the will of the one to be purged. From countless such lines we gather Pelagians and Semipelagians agreed never to grant God’s special munificence by which faith and charity are poured into some and a good will is thereby created in them. For a makeweight add this: Arminius, Arnoldus, and the rest from that school do not acknowledge the grace Pelagians and Semipelagians rejected—the grace that by its efficacy makes the good will—but only the grace that by persuasion moves the will to want to be good, and leaves the event to free will.

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1 Arminius parallel: Exam. Perkins — soft persuasion not coercion; same Pelagian calumny; Corvinus leaves the will at the fork
latin: Atque hinc est quod ex praescientia Dei, qua ab aeterno cognoscit velitne homo gratiam pulsantem intromittere an secus, procedere statuant electionem et reprobationem. Audiamus ipsum Arminium, Exam. Praedest. Perkin. pag. 220. Gratiae Autor statuit per gratiam suam non cogere homines ad assentiendum, sed leni et suavi suasione movere. Hoc idem est quod concessit Pelagius: Suadet omne quod bonum est. Illud etiam observandum: Innuere Arminium, Si Divina gratia aliter agat quam per hanc lenem suasionem, qua eventum relinquit libero arbitrio, illam protinus cogere voluntatem: quae fuit ipsissima Pelagii et Semipelagianorum calumnia. Sed Arminio jungamus etiam Corvinum; qui aliam gratiam non agnoscit, praeter eam quae voluntatem in bivio quasi positam relinquit, ita ut si voluntas suo actu in id feratur ad quod allicit gratia, tum homo convertatur; sin secus, inexcusabilis relinquatur.
pass_a: And hence it is that from God’s foresight, by which from eternity he knows whether a man will let in knocking grace or not, they establish that election and reprobation proceed. Let us hear Arminius himself, Exam. Praedest. Perkin. pag. 220. The Author of grace has established by his grace not to compel men unto assenting, but to move them by gentle and sweet persuasion. This is the same which Pelagius granted: He persuades everything that is good. That also is to be observed: that Arminius hints that If Divine grace act otherwise than by this gentle persuasion, by which it leaves the event unto free will, it at once compels the will: which was the very calumny of Pelagius and the Semipelagians. But let us join Corvinus also unto Arminius; who acknowledges no other grace than that which leaves the will as it were set at a fork, so that if the will by its own act is carried unto that unto which grace allures, then the man is converted; but if otherwise, he is left inexcusable.
pass_b: Hence they let election and reprobation proceed from God’s foresight of whether a man will admit knocking grace or not. Hear Arminius himself (Exam. Praedest. Perkins, p. 220): The Author of grace has set that by his grace he will not compel men to assent, but move them by gentle, sweet persuasion. That is what Pelagius granted: He persuades all that is good. Note also Arminius’s hint: if divine grace acts otherwise than by this soft persuasion that leaves the event to free will, it at once compels the will—the very calumny of Pelagius and the Semipelagians. Join Corvinus to Arminius: he acknowledges no grace but what leaves the will at a fork—so that if the will by its own act goes where grace allures, the man is converted; if not, he is left without excuse.

lemmas.gloss: Corvinus: will left at the fork
